You are implementing one GitHub issue in BrokkAi/bifrost-dev (the repository is cloned at `bifrost/`). Read `bifrost/AGENTS.md` first and follow it. In particular:

- Assign the issue to yourself and add the `agent-in-progress` label before starting (`gh issue edit N --add-assignee @me --add-label agent-in-progress`). Remove the label if you stand down without resolving it.
- Read the issue with all comments: `gh issue view N --comments`. The comments hold measurements and revised plans that override the issue body where they differ.
- `.agents/docs/*` files are point-in-time records; recheck any claim from them against the code before relying on it.
- Commit directly to `master`, only the files you changed, with a clear multiline message. Push to `origin/master`. If the push is rejected, `git fetch`, `git merge origin/master` (never rebase), rerun the affected tests, push again. If pushing is impossible (no credentials), leave your commits on the local branch and say so in your final message; do not open a PR.
- Build with plain `cargo`; do not set or redirect `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Keep validation proportional: `cargo fmt`, the two clippy commands from `.agents/docs/testing-and-rust-validation.md`, and `cargo nextest run --max-fail 100 -p <crate>` for the affected crates, with `BIFROST_PARALLELISM=1 RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_HOME` cleared. Run the whole test suite only if your change touches a shared path whose consumers extend beyond the crate.
- Other sessions are working concurrently on issues #3748, #3749, #3751, #3755, #3761, #3762, #3763, #3764 (and later #3754, #3756). Stay inside your issue's scope; do not refactor code those issues own. If you find a bug outside your scope, file an issue instead of fixing it.
- Check `nproc` and available memory first and size benchmark runs to the machine. Prefer existing `BIFROST_TIMING=1` spans and the MCP stdio server for measurements; the `benchmark/` harness is available too.
- You may delegate research, independent verification, or a second opinion on a design to your subagent, which runs a different model. Use it for review of your diff before you push.
- When done: comment on the issue with the landed commit SHA(s), what changed, exactly which validation ran, before/after measurements where the issue's acceptance asks for them, and any follow-ups. Close the issue only if its acceptance criteria are met; otherwise leave it open and state what remains. Finish with a short final message to me: outcome, commit, open questions. If you are blocked, stop and say so rather than widening scope.

Issue: #3749 (early cutoff on the update path). Plan step 1 already landed (34fa615c1). Your scope, in this order:

1. go.mod semantic digest (plan step 2 in the issue, about 3 s per require-only edit on kubernetes, measured in the comments). Parse `go.mod`; if the module path is unchanged, call the ordinary update path instead of `update_all`, and record the new byte digest. First check that Go dependency-pack consumers invalidate on `require` changes through their own keys. Extend the go.mod update test near `usages/get_definition/go.rs:7300-7330` with a require-only edit: assert no full reconcile and results equal to a fresh build. Land this as its own commit.

2. Incremental Rust crate derivation. The measurements show a fixed about 34 s to re-derive a large crate on any edit inside it (`collect_rows` 24 s, `export_declarations` 4 s, `import_resolution` 1.9 s, `root_references` 1.8 s, `publication` 1.7 s in `store/rust_crates.rs`), regardless of the edited file's size. Investigate whether `collect_rows` (first) can reuse per-file results for unchanged member blobs, keeping the crate rows identical to a fresh derivation. Use the existing `a_scoped_reconcile_publishes_what_the_full_pass_would` test as the model for an incremental-versus-fresh check. If a bounded implementation is feasible, implement it and measure a body edit inside `crates/bifrost-analysis` (a large crate) before and after, using an MCP session with the real watcher (write the edit, wait 2 s, issue a request); use a distinct literal per edit so the blob is new. If it is not feasible within the crate's design, write up why on the issue with the specific obstacle, and stop.

3. Do NOT implement plan step 4 (fragment-keyed usage graph). The measurements show the whole-workspace `usage_graph` is recomputed on every call, so there is no reusable graph to invalidate. Instead, post one comment on the issue summarizing whether the graph should become reusable across requests, as a question for the owner, with the tradeoff against the heap-residency rule in AGENTS.md.

**Commits** (merged into master as 8d434d4b3c):
- 6e9847e18c: a go.mod edit that keeps the module path is now an ordinary incremental update.
- 998d5c5e26: the Rust crate-derivation fix.

**1. go.mod digest.** I checked first that dependency packs don't depend on `update_all`: the MCP host already refreshes them for any changed go.mod.
- A new adapter hook reports what an input contributes to package identity. For Go that is the parsed module path.
- An edit that keeps it takes the ordinary update path and records the new byte digest, so content-keyed caches still move.
- Every other language, including Cargo.toml, keeps the old behavior. #3754 can plug a Cargo.toml digest into this same hook.
- The extended test asserts that a require-only edit runs no full rebuild and matches a fresh build. A reviewer confirmed it would have failed on the old code.
- I did not re-measure the kubernetes edit; the issue's figure is about 3 s before the change.

**2. Rust crate derivation.** The fixed ~34 s was not per-file work. It was one bad query plan: the root-references SELECT scanned a temp view once per reference, 177,237 references against about 2,200 modules. That view is now a keyed temp table, and a plan pin guards it.

Measured with the real watcher, a body edit in `crates/bifrost-analysis`, 3 edits each:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Request after the edit | 91–102 s | 25–28 s |
| That one SELECT | 62–70 s | 0.7–0.9 s |

- **Rows unchanged:** all 239,694 crate rows were identical between the old and new code's derivations of the same crate.
- **Noisy host:** other sessions pushed the load average to about 220 on 96 CPUs, so absolute times are inflated. The before and after runs were back to back.
- **Per-file reuse:** I did not attempt it for the remaining ~25 s, because it would need a schema redesign. The issue comment gives the specific obstacles.

**3. Usage graph.** I posted the question on the issue, with a recommendation. Keep `usage_graph` per request for now. If reuse is ever needed, store per-file edge fragments as rows in SQLite, since a large retained graph in memory would break the heap-residency rule.

#3754 is done and closed. A Cargo.toml edit that keeps the manifest's meaning now skips `update_all`. Measured through the real watcher, a comment-only edit to the analysis crate's Cargo.toml went from about 1.7 s of update time to about 0.1 s. Commit 94842134a7 is pushed to master in merge b1be106562, and the table is posted on the issue.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `WorkspaceAnalyzer::update` | 1.60 / 1.67 / 1.85 s | 0.11 / 0.08 / 0.08 s |
| Request after the edit | 2.15 / 2.17 / 2.39 s | 0.67 / 0.56 / 0.59 s |

Other sessions shared the host, with a load average of about 80 to 130 on 96 CPUs, so absolute times are inflated. The before and after runs were back to back.

**How it works:**
- **Digest.** The Rust adapter plugs into the hook I added in #3749. It hashes the parsed manifest from the same parser crate reconcile uses, so comments, whitespace and key order drop out.
- **Why it covers more than your field list.** It is a denylist: it leaves out only what no Rust reader consumes, meaning `[profile]`, `[badges]`, `metadata` tables and publishing fields such as description and version. Everything else counts, because crate inventory also reads features, dependency feature lists and target names, and Cargo routes read `[target.*]` tables and `[patch]`. A manifest that fails to parse still rebuilds on any edit.
- **An extra step you didn't ask for.** Skipping `update_all` alone would have left the old manifest bytes in the store, and crate reconcile reads manifests from there. A new store method republishes the one manifest. The crate reconcile also leaves that manifest out of its changed paths; otherwise any `.toml` path forces a pass over all 144 crates. On the real store after the benchmark, the retained Cargo.toml matched the disk and the crate rows were current at head.

**Tests:**
- The comment-only scenario and a new description/version/`[profile]`/reformat scenario assert no full rebuild. They also check that the stored manifest bytes and the crate rows' current marker match a fresh build.
- The rename and new-path-dependency scenarios assert exactly one rebuild and still match a fresh build.
- Unit tests pin what the digest ignores and what it follows.
- I changed the test-only rebuild counter from thread-local to keyed by project root. Workspace delegates update on rayon threads, so a thread-local counter would miss them.

**Validation:** fmt and both clippy commands are clean. The `brokk-bifrost-analysis` and `brokk-bifrost-rust` suites passed 5,292 of 5,293. The one failure is the known load-sensitive blast-radius test, #3476, which passed alone. After merging origin/master, which had changed two of my files for #3763, the 74 affected tests passed.

There are no open questions on #3754. The usage-graph question on #3749 still needs your decision.
